storm.summary_layperson: No storm threat for the cove tonight — skies are clear to mostly sunny with nothing on radar, and instability is too weak for thunderstorms to organize.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air-water gap is already down to just 2°F, below the 5°F needed for a protective marine layer — but with no storms approaching, there's nothing for the Sound to blunt either way.
storm.detail_html:
Today's OKX forecast discussion mentions only a slight, non-zero chance of an isolated or embedded thunderstorm toward evening as a weak upper-level trough passes overhead, but the numbers don't support anything organized: HRRR shows CAPE (a measure of atmospheric instability) of just 70–110 J/kg through the window, far below the roughly 1500 J/kg threshold where storms typically start punching through. Radar out of KOKX shows zero active cells anywhere in the region right now.

The marine-layer buffer that sometimes weakens storms before they reach the cove isn't a factor either way tonight. The Sound is running 75°F against 77°F air — a 2°F gap, already below the roughly 5°F threshold this mechanism needs to matter. The protective mechanism is not active, but since there's no storm inbound to buffer, that's a non-issue rather than a risk.

Bottom line for the 5–10 PM window: quiet and low-risk. No NWS watches or advisories are posted for the area.

What would change this call: any new cells developing over the Hudson Valley or western Connecticut later this evening, or OKX upgrading its "possible thunderstorm" language to an active advisory. Nothing in the current data points that direction.

wind.tactics_blurb: Expect a fading northeast breeze through the evening — around 6–7 kt at 5 PM, dropping to light-and-variable by 9–10 PM; be ready for a drifter finish. Favor the center of the course since direction is unsettled rather than committing to one side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-only day, not a sea-breeze day: the air–water temperature difference (the "deltaT" that drives a thermal sea breeze) is only 2.2°F, well under the roughly 5°F gate needed, and 0% of coastal stations are showing the southerly flow that marks an active sea breeze. There's no thermal component in play tonight — whatever wind you feel is straight synoptic (gradient) flow.

Right now (mid-afternoon) the cove is seeing a solid breeze — RYC reads 10.9 kt gusting 15.5 — and the broader station ensemble averages 9.4 kt, which would normally put today in the moderate-gradient bracket. But HRRR's hour-by-hour forecast shows this fading fast: 6.8 kt at 5 PM, 6.1 kt at 6 PM, 4.7 kt by 7 PM, well beyond the mild 1–2 kt overnight softening a typical moderate-gradient day sees. Because most of the 5–10 PM window is forecast in the sub-8-kt range, this window is called as the lighter sub-type rather than the current-hour reading.

Direction is the bigger flag: HRRR forecasts a backing NE-to-ENE flow, but current stations on the west side of the course (including RYC) are already reading ESE — a 70° divergence — and agreement across the station ensemble is low (0.44 out of 1.0, versus the 0.7 threshold that usually signals a settled flow). That combination points to an unsettled, possibly locally-eddying breeze rather than a clean synoptic direction, so there's no strong geography read (like the S–SW or S–SE axis calls in the cove's geography table) to favor one side of the course.

HRRR's own forecast run out only through 7 PM this cycle (later hours failed to fetch); the 8–10 PM values above are extrapolated from the model's own decay trend, not direct model output, so treat the back half of the window as lower-confidence. Given the trajectory, fleets should expect a genuinely light, possibly sub-3-kt finish by 9–10 PM — plan for a drifter, not a breeze-on evening.
